notes.definition: Sodium hydroxide solution is used to identify some metal ions (cations) in solution, because many metal ions form insoluble hydroxides with characteristic colours: white for Al³⁺, Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ (only Al(OH)₃ dissolves in excess), blue for Cu²⁺, green for Fe²⁺ and brown for Fe³⁺.
explanation: To test for metal ions, dissolve the solid in water (if needed) and put a small amount of the solution in a test tube. Add a few drops of dilute sodium hydroxide solution using a dropping pipette. If the metal hydroxide is insoluble, a solid precipitate forms. Its colour helps identify the metal ion. Then add more sodium hydroxide (an excess) and see whether the precipitate dissolves.

Aluminium (Al³⁺), calcium (Ca²⁺) and magnesium (Mg²⁺) ions all form white precipitates. Only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves when excess sodium hydroxide is added, giving a colourless solution again; this distinguishes aluminium from the other two. Calcium and magnesium cannot be told apart with sodium hydroxide alone, but a flame test can separate them: calcium gives an orange-red flame and magnesium gives no colour.

Transition metal ions give coloured precipitates. Copper(II) ions (Cu²⁺) give a blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide. Iron(II) ions (Fe²⁺) give a green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide; this can slowly turn brown at the surface as it reacts with oxygen in the air. Iron(III) ions (Fe³⁺) give a brown (orange-brown) precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide.

You should be able to write balanced equations for forming the insoluble hydroxides. For example, CuSO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s) + Na₂SO₄(aq) and FeCl₃(aq) + 3NaOH(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s) + 3NaCl(aq). The number of hydroxide ions in the formula equals the charge on the metal ion: Cu²⁺ needs two OH⁻ and Fe³⁺ needs three. Higher tier students should also write ionic equations, which show only the ions that react, such as Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s). The sodium ions and the negative ion from the original compound are spectator ions.

Required practical 7 is about using chemical tests to identify the ions in unknown single ionic compounds. The positive ion is identified by a flame test or by sodium hydroxide solution. The negative ion is identified using dilute acid and limewater (carbonate), dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate solution (halides: white, cream or yellow precipitate) or dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride solution (sulfate: white precipitate). Combining the results names the compound, for example a blue precipitate with NaOH and a white precipitate with barium chloride shows copper(II) sulfate.
keyFacts: Add a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution, then excess.
Al³⁺: white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH.
Ca²⁺: white precipitate, does not dissolve in excess.
Mg²⁺: white precipitate, does not dissolve in excess.
Use a flame test to tell Ca²⁺ (orange-red) from Mg²⁺ (no colour).
Number of OH⁻ in the hydroxide = charge on the metal ion: Cu(OH)₂, Fe(OH)₃.
Required practical 7 combines flame tests, NaOH, carbonate, halide and sulfate tests to identify an ionic compound.

keyTerms.definition: An insoluble solid formed when two solutions react.
More of a reagent than is needed to react completely; here, adding plenty of sodium hydroxide.
A positively charged ion, such as a metal ion.
A compound of a metal ion with hydroxide ions (OH⁻), such as Cu(OH)₂.
An equation showing only the ions and substances that take part in the reaction, leaving out spectator ions.
An ion present in the solution that does not take part in the reaction, such as Na⁺ here.

equations.formula: copper(II) sulfate + sodium hydroxide → copper(II) hydroxide + sodium sulfate

equations.name: Iron(III) hydroxide precipitate
equations.formula: iron(III) chloride + sodium hydroxide → iron(III) hydroxide + sodium chloride

equations.name: General ionic equation (HT)
equations.formula: metal ion + hydroxide ions → metal hydroxide

workedExamples.title: Identifying an ion from precipitate results
workedExamples.question: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to solution X. A white precipitate forms, which dissolves when excess sodium hydroxide is added. Identify the metal ion.
steps: White precipitates form with Al³⁺, Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺.
Only aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide.

workedExamples.title: Writing a balanced equation
workedExamples.question: Write a balanced equation for the reaction between iron(II) sulfate solution and sodium hydroxide solution.
steps: Iron(II) is Fe²⁺, so its hydroxide is Fe(OH)₂ (two OH⁻ balance the 2+ charge).
Sulfate is SO₄²⁻, so sodium sulfate is Na₂SO₄.
FeSO₄ + NaOH → Fe(OH)₂ + Na₂SO₄. Two OH and two Na are needed on the right, so put 2 in front of NaOH.
Add state symbols: the hydroxide is the solid precipitate.

workedExamples.title: Writing an ionic equation (Higher)
workedExamples.question: Write the ionic equation for the formation of the precipitate when sodium hydroxide is added to magnesium chloride solution.
steps: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are in solution on both sides, so they are spectator ions and are removed.
Only Mg²⁺ and OH⁻ react to form the solid.

workedExamples.title: Identifying a compound (required practical 7)
workedExamples.question: Solid Y dissolves in water. With sodium hydroxide, a brown precipitate forms. With dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate solution, a white precipitate forms. Name Y.
steps: Brown precipitate with NaOH shows iron(III) ions, Fe³⁺.
White precipitate with acidified silver nitrate shows chloride ions, Cl⁻.
Fe³⁺ and Cl⁻ combine as FeCl₃.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all white precipitates mean the same ion.
misconceptions.right: In fact Al³⁺, Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ all give white precipitates. Adding excess NaOH identifies aluminium (dissolves); a flame test separates calcium (orange-red) from magnesium (no colour).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often mix up iron(II) and iron(III): 'iron(II) gives brown'.
misconceptions.right: In fact Fe²⁺ gives a green precipitate and Fe³⁺ gives a brown precipitate.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write copper hydroxide as CuOH or iron(III) hydroxide as Fe(OH)₂.
misconceptions.right: In fact the number of OH⁻ ions equals the metal ion's charge: Cu(OH)₂ and Fe(OH)₃.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often include Na⁺ in ionic equations.
misconceptions.right: In fact Na⁺ is a spectator ion. The ionic equation is just the metal ion plus hydroxide ions forming the solid.

realWorld: Water companies test water for dissolved iron and aluminium ions, which can come from pipes and treatment chemicals.
Forensic and environmental chemists use these quick tests to screen samples before more accurate instrumental analysis.
Precipitating metal hydroxides by adding alkali is used to remove toxic metal ions from industrial waste water.
higherTier: Ionic equations for forming the precipitates, for example Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s), Fe²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₂(s), Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s), Al³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Al(OH)₃(s).
separateOnlyContent: Identifying metal ions with sodium hydroxide solution, and required practical 7 (identifying ions), are in separate Chemistry only (8462).
examTips: Learn the table: white (Al, Ca, Mg), blue (Cu²⁺), green (Fe²⁺), brown (Fe³⁺). Remember 'Al dissolves in excess'.
When describing the test, say 'add a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution, then excess'.
To balance hydroxide formulae, match the number of OH⁻ to the charge on the metal ion.
For identification questions, combine evidence: positive ion from NaOH or flame test, negative ion from carbonate, halide or sulfate tests.
In ionic equations include state symbols, with (s) on the precipitate.
summary: NaOH solution forms insoluble hydroxide precipitates with many metal ions.
White: Al³⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ (only Al(OH)₃ dissolves in excess).
Blue: Cu²⁺. Green: Fe²⁺. Brown: Fe³⁺.
Use a flame test to tell Ca²⁺ from Mg²⁺.
Write balanced equations; Higher tier also ionic equations.
Required practical 7 combines tests to identify an ionic compound.

questions.question: What colour precipitate forms when sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution containing copper(II) ions?
markScheme: 1 mark: Blue
questions.explanation: Copper(II) hydroxide is blue. Green is iron(II) and brown is iron(III).

questions.question: Which metal ion forms a brown precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: Iron(III)
questions.explanation: Iron(III) hydroxide is brown. Iron(II) hydroxide is green.

questions.question: Which metal ion forms a green precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: Iron(II)
questions.explanation: Iron(II) hydroxide is green; iron(III) is brown; magnesium and aluminium give white.

questions.question: A white precipitate forms with a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution and dissolves in excess. Which ion is present?
markScheme: 1 mark: Aluminium
questions.explanation: Of the three white precipitates, only aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide.

questions.question: Which test distinguishes calcium ions from magnesium ions?
markScheme: 1 mark: A flame test
questions.explanation: Both give white precipitates that do not dissolve in excess NaOH. A flame test shows orange-red for calcium and no colour for magnesium.

questions.question: What is the formula of iron(III) hydroxide?
markScheme: 1 mark: Fe(OH)₃
questions.explanation: Fe³⁺ needs three OH⁻ ions to balance its charge.

questions.question: Which is the correct ionic equation for the reaction of iron(II) sulfate solution with sodium hydroxide solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: Fe²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₂(s)
questions.explanation: Only Fe²⁺ and OH⁻ react; Na⁺ and SO₄²⁻ are spectator ions.

questions.question: Which balanced equation is correct?
markScheme: 1 mark: AlCl₃ + 3NaOH → Al(OH)₃ + 3NaCl
questions.explanation: Al³⁺ forms Al(OH)₃, so three NaOH are needed, giving three NaCl.

questions.question: Required practical 7: a solution gives a blue precipitate with sodium hydroxide and a white precipitate with dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride. What is the compound?
markScheme: 1 mark: Copper(II) sulfate
questions.explanation: Blue precipitate shows Cu²⁺; white precipitate with acidified barium chloride shows SO₄²⁻.

questions.question: What is the name for an insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed?
markScheme: 1 mark: Precipitate
questions.explanation: A precipitate is the insoluble solid that forms in a reaction between solutions.

questions.question: Describe how to test a solution for metal ions using sodium hydroxide.
acceptedAnswers: add a few drops of sodium hydroxide
markScheme: 1 mark: add a few drops of (dilute) sodium hydroxide solution
1 mark: observe the colour of any precipitate (then add excess and see if it dissolves)
questions.explanation: The precipitate colour and its behaviour in excess identify the ion.

questions.question: Give the colour of the precipitate formed with sodium hydroxide solution for: (a) Cu²⁺, (b) Fe²⁺, (c) Fe³⁺.
markScheme: 1 mark: Cu²⁺ blue
1 mark: Fe²⁺ green
1 mark: Fe³⁺ brown
questions.explanation: These three colours are required knowledge.

questions.question: Explain how you could use sodium hydroxide solution to tell aluminium ions from magnesium ions.
markScheme: 1 mark: both give a white precipitate with a few drops
1 mark: add excess NaOH: the aluminium precipitate dissolves, the magnesium precipitate does not
questions.explanation: Excess sodium hydroxide is the key step for aluminium.

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction between copper(II) sulfate solution and sodium hydroxide solution.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct formulae CuSO₄, NaOH, Cu(OH)₂, Na₂SO₄
1 mark: correctly balanced with 2NaOH
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ needs two OH⁻; Na₂SO₄ also needs two Na⁺.

questions.question: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction between iron(III) chloride solution and sodium hydroxide solution.
markScheme: 1 mark: Fe³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₃
1 mark: correct state symbols (aq), (aq), (s)
questions.explanation: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions and are left out.

questions.question: Name the spectator ions when sodium hydroxide solution is added to magnesium chloride solution, and explain why they are spectator ions.
markScheme: 1 mark: Na⁺ and Cl⁻
1 mark: they remain dissolved in solution / do not change during the reaction
questions.explanation: Only Mg²⁺ and OH⁻ combine to form the solid Mg(OH)₂.

questions.question: A solution gives a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide that does not dissolve in excess. Give the two metal ions that could be present and describe a further test to identify which one it is.
markScheme: 1 mark: calcium (Ca²⁺) or magnesium (Mg²⁺)
1 mark: flame test: orange-red shows calcium; no colour shows magnesium
questions.explanation: Sodium hydroxide alone cannot distinguish these two.

questions.question: A green precipitate forms when sodium hydroxide is added to a solution. After being left in air, the top of the precipitate turns brown. Suggest an explanation.
markScheme: 1 mark: the solution contains iron(II) ions (green Fe(OH)₂)
1 mark: oxygen in the air oxidises iron(II) hydroxide to iron(III) hydroxide, which is brown
questions.explanation: This explains why iron(II) precipitates can look brownish if left standing.

questions.question: Required practical 7: a white solid gives a crimson flame and fizzes with dilute acid, producing a gas that turns limewater milky. Name the solid.
markScheme: 1 mark: lithium (crimson flame)
1 mark: carbonate (CO₂ with acid): lithium carbonate
questions.explanation: Combine the metal-ion and negative-ion tests to name the compound.

questions.question: A student has solutions of three compounds: copper(II) chloride, iron(II) sulfate and iron(III) nitrate. Describe how the student could use sodium hydroxide solution to identify each solution.
markScheme: Indicative content: put a small sample of each solution in a test tube
Add a few drops of dilute sodium hydroxide solution
Copper(II): blue precipitate
Iron(II): green precipitate
Iron(III): brown precipitate
Use clean test tubes / small volumes / eye protection
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): method and all three correct observations linked to ions
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two correct observations or a simple method
questions.explanation: Each metal ion gives a distinctively coloured hydroxide precipitate.

questions.question:
Required practical 7: a student is given five unlabelled white solids: aluminium sulfate, calcium chloride, magnesium sulfate, sodium carbonate and potassium bromide.
Plan a series of chemical tests that would identify every solid. Give the expected results.
markScheme: Indicative content: dissolve each solid in water
Flame test on each: sodium yellow (sodium carbonate), potassium lilac (potassium bromide), calcium orange-red (calcium chloride); aluminium and magnesium no colour
Add NaOH: aluminium, calcium, magnesium give white precipitates; aluminium dissolves in excess
So aluminium sulfate: white precipitate dissolving in excess; magnesium sulfate: white precipitate, insoluble in excess, no flame colour
Carbonate: add dilute acid, fizzing; gas turns limewater milky (sodium carbonate)
Halide: add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate: cream precipitate (bromide)
Chloride: white precipitate with acidified silver nitrate (calcium chloride)
Sulfate: dilute hydrochloric acid then barium chloride: white precipitate (aluminium sulfate and magnesium sulfate)
Logical order and use of results to eliminate possibilities
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): coherent plan identifying all five with correct reagents and results for both ions
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): tests that identify at least three solids with mostly correct results
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant tests and results
questions.explanation: Strong answers use both positive and negative ion tests and explain how each result narrows down the possibilities.

questions.question: Solution Z gives a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide that does not dissolve in excess, and gives no colour in a flame test. Which ion is in Z?
markScheme: 1 mark: Magnesium
questions.explanation: White and insoluble in excess means calcium or magnesium; no flame colour rules out calcium (orange-red).

questions.question: Which reagent is used to identify metal ions such as Cu²⁺ and Fe³⁺ in solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: Sodium hydroxide solution
questions.explanation: Sodium hydroxide forms coloured hydroxide precipitates with these ions.

questions.question: Name the ion that gives a blue precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution.
markScheme: 1 mark: copper(II) ion / Cu²⁺
questions.explanation: Copper(II) hydroxide is blue.

questions.question: A student adds sodium hydroxide solution to a solution containing both Fe³⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions. What would the student most likely see?
options: A brown precipitate, which may hide the white one
markScheme: 1 mark: A brown precipitate, which may hide the white one
questions.explanation: Both hydroxides precipitate, but the brown Fe(OH)₃ masks the white Mg(OH)₂. This is why the tests work best on single compounds.

questions.question: Explain why it is important to add sodium hydroxide a few drops at a time before adding excess when testing for aluminium ions.
markScheme: 1 mark: so that the white precipitate is seen forming first
1 mark: adding excess at once could dissolve aluminium hydroxide immediately, so no precipitate would be seen
questions.explanation: Seeing both stages (precipitate, then dissolving) is what identifies aluminium.
